This is game 21 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If AGENTS.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session (its first 64 KiB); your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

## This game

A new game. You play Black, so you move first.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
I’ll stay at 20k while working toward repeatable wins. As Black, I’ll count area early, check eye boundaries during fights, and save every returned position.

# Game 20: White vs 20k — B+16

Resumed on 2026-10-05 and completed on 2026-10-06. 9×9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Consecutive passes at moves 66–67 ended the game. Final captures: Black 8, White 1.
The 20k series record is four wins, eleven losses and one draw. Retain 20k.

## Record scope and verified score

This session began after Black move 19 (C4), with White to play move 20. The earlier session had saved no game-020 files. The exposed tools return the current board, not move history. Moves 1–19 cannot be recovered in their original order.

- game-020.sgf begins with exact AB/AW setup after move 19, PL[W], and records moves 20–67, starting with MN[20]. It is a continuation record, not an invented complete opening.
- game-020-log.json contains the resumed board and all 24 play responses, current-board group/liberty/empty-region inventories, all 48 continuation moves, decision notes, final row count and record validation.
- The continuation contains 45 stone moves and three passes (63, 66, 67). From initial stone/capture totals, the first 19 moves were stone moves; the whole game therefore had 67 moves, 64 stone moves and three passes, although the first 19 move coordinates in sequence are unavailable.
- Historical replay of the actual continuation reproduced all 24 returned boards and final captures. The initial White capture was already present at resumption.
- Official and independent result agree: Black 52, White 29 + 7 = 36, B+16.
- Black 31 stones + 21 territory; White 24 stones + five territory. No neutral points or additional scoring removal. The final scoring board equals the last playing board.
- Black area by rows 1–9: 5, 6, 6, 9, 7, 6, 5, 4, 4 = 52.
- White area by rows 1–9: 4, 3, 3, 0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5 = 29.
- All move choices and hypothetical reading were manual. Code inspected current positions, counted liberties/area, kept records, converted the continuation to SGF and checked historical replay. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation.

## Starting position and strategic deficit

Black: C4/D4/E4, F2/F3, G4/H4, E1, F6.
White: C3 and F1/G1/G2/G3/H1/H3/J2/J3.

The eight-stone lower-right group was already unconditionally alive:
- H2 boundaries G2/H1/H3/J2, all one connected White group.
- J1 boundaries H1/J2, same White group.
It secured ten area. Preserve both eyes; the remaining board needed at least 28 additional White area for a win if all points were assigned.

C3 had B3/C2/D3 liberties and no established base. Black's C4/D4/E4 wall and lower F/E stones already constrained its central and right routes. The resumed session opened at C7/D7 instead of immediately developing C3. That expanded another foothold but did not resolve the lower base.

20 W C7, 21 B C6, 22 W D7, 23 B E7,
24 W C2, 25 B B2, 26 W D2, 27 B C8,
28 W D8, 29 B E2, 30 W B3, 31 B D1,
32 W A3, 33 B D3.

B2 undercut the left corner. E2 joined E1 to F2/F3; D1 joined that group rather than remain capturable. D3 joined the central wall and closed the lower group's perpendicular route. The initial idea of reaching the living right group through an E1 capture was no longer available.

Reconsider before B2/E2/D1/D3 close these routes, and before spending more lower moves on a trapped enemy capture. Earlier B3/B4, earlier lower development instead of C7/D7, or E2 before Black E2 are hypotheses only. No saving or winning replacement was verified.

## Lower-left: winning a small capture would still leave one eye

34 W A2, 35 B B1, 36 W C1, 37 B B4,
38 W A4, 39 B A5.

A2 ataried B2 at B1. Black B1 extended to A1/C1. White C1 joined C2 and ataried B1/B2 at A1, but Black B4 closed the outside route. The seven-stone White group then had only A1/A4. White A4 extended with only new A5; Black A5 removed that liberty.

After move 39:
- White A2/A3/A4/B3/C1/C2/C3/D2: eight stones, only A1.
- Black B1/B2: only A1.
- This is neither seki nor ko.

Manual proof on this position:
W A1 captures two and makes a nine-stone White group with exactly B1/B2.
B B1 invades that two-point eye space. W B2 captures the one Black B1 stone, but the resulting ten-stone White group has only B1.
B B1 captures all ten. The emptied A1/B2/C1 points give the capturer liberties; they do not automatically connect it to B4. No ko is involved.

Even the immediate W A1 capture after move 37 would not establish life: B A4 would close the last outside liberty and leave only B1/B2. Thus adding A4 did not solve an already inadequate eye-space plan.

White abandoned the dead group at move 40 rather than fill A1. Black A1 at move 53 physically captured the eight original stones. The returned capture count increased from zero to eight, agreeing with the diagnosis.

The actionable mistake is earlier: choosing moves to capture B1/B2 without retaining enough outside space for a second eye. B4 before C1 or before the A2/B1 exchanges is an unverified candidate to retain an escape. A raw liberty inventory correctly described the danger but was acted on too late.

## Upper rescue: real connections around G8

40 W E8, 41 B B7, 42 W F8, 43 B G7,
44 W H6, 45 B F7, 46 W H7, 47 B G8,
48 W G9, 49 B D6, 50 W H9, 51 B C9,
52 W H8, 53 B A1, 54 W F9, 55 B D9,
56 W G6, 57 B G5, 58 W H5, 59 B J4.

E8/F8 connected the upper-left stones but did not create eyes. H6/H7 established a right-side foothold while that side remained open. Black G8 cut the direct connection.

G9 initially had F9/H9. The possible B F9 cut was read manually: F9 would have only E9, and W E9 could join E8 and capture it, reopening F9 for G9. This alternative was not played, and it is not evidence of a forced winning upper plan.

Actual H9 joined G9; H8 joined H9 to H7/H6; F9 then joined the entire upper chain through F8/G9. Every connection was orthogonal. This preserved C7/D7/D8/E8/F8 without assuming the top strip already had eyes.

A rough target recorded after move 43 was incorrectly added as D–F rows 8/9 (6), G–J rows 5–9 (20), C7/D7 (2): 28 upper potential plus ten lower-right = 38. Review found the arithmetic error: G–J contains only G/H/J, THREE columns because I is skipped. Those five rows contain fifteen points, so the corrected target was only 23 upper + ten lower-right = 33, already insufficient even if fully retained. It also included contested Black G7 and depended on recovering that point; it was an aspirational region, not owned territory. The final upper region was nineteen. Use explicit coordinate sets or row counts for every outline, not alphabetic-span intuition.

## Upper life proof and rejected false threat

60 W J5, 61 B E5, 62 W J7, 63 B pass,
64 W E9, 65 B B8, 66 W pass, 67 B pass.

J5 secured the lower endpoint of J6–J9. J7 divided that space:
- J6 boundaries H6/J5/J7.
- J8/J9 boundaries H8/H9/J7.
All boundaries were in one connected White group. These are separate unconditional eye spaces. E9 then joined E8/F9, securing the last mixed boundary point while preserving both eyes.

Upper: sixteen stones + J6/J8/J9 = nineteen area.
Lower-right: eight stones + H2/J1 = ten area.
Total 29, still nine points below White's minimum winning area of 38. An eight-point shift from Black to White would draw at 44–37; nine would win at 43–38.

The final central Black E7/F6/F7/G7/G8 group had only E6/F5, but either could connect it to other Black stones. It was not a trapped two-liberty group with a forced capture.

The rejected White F5 threat is a concrete success in applying game 18's lesson. After Black E5, White F5 would atari the central group at E6 and the right G4/G5/H4/J4 group at F4. But White F5 itself would have only F4. Black F4 would join G4/F3/E4, capture F5 immediately and reopen that point for the threatened groups. Two ataris would not make the threat forcing. This was read manually and not played.

## Carry forward

1. Retain 20k: four wins, eleven losses, one draw. Life and sufficient area remain separate tests.
2. Before pursuing a corner capture, prove its resulting eye space and preserve an outside route. C1 ataried two stones, but B4/A5 left the main group dead; capturing at A1 would supply only one two-point eye.
3. Keep actual upper connections G9–H9–H8 and F9–F8, and the explicit J5/J7 life proof. The played rescue secured nineteen area; it was not a winning framework.
4. Count Go columns explicitly: G–J is G/H/J, three columns. The claimed 38-point target was actually 33, already below White's winning threshold. The final 52–29 count was independently verified.
5. Keep rejecting threats the opponent can answer by capturing their new stone. F5's two ataris failed because Black F4 would capture it first.
6. Save records during play, especially before a session ends. This continuation is exact, but the unsaved opening order is permanently missing from the available record.

# Game 17: Black vs 20k — B+8

Played 2026-10-05. 9×9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 86–87: 87 moves, 85 stone moves.
Final captures: Black 16, White 2. No invalid move or resignation.
The final scoring display matches the last playing board; no further dead-stone removal was needed.

The 20k record is now four wins, eight losses and one draw. Retain 20k. Both Black footholds lived, and sufficient area was counted before passing. Important territorial gains still depended on ignored ataris; this is not a forced opening win.

## Records and verified result

- game-017.sgf contains all 87 moves.
- game-017-log.json contains all 44 play responses, complete moves, returned-board group/liberty inventories, counting notes and the independent final count. Inventories for the first four responses were reconstructed after play; subsequent inventories were inspected during play.
- Official result and independent count agree: Black 48, White 33 plus 7 komi = 40, B+8.
- Black: 41 stones + 7 territory. White: 26 stones + 7 territory. No neutral points.
- Black area by rows 1–9: 9, 8, 6, 4, 6, 6, 4, 3, 2 = 48.
- White area by rows 1–9: 0, 1, 3, 5, 3, 3, 5, 6, 7 = 33.
- Black territory: A1, A3/A4, C2, E1, J6, J8.
- White territory: A8, B7, B9, C8, D7, D9, E8.

## Opening: three footholds, then actual lower connections

1 B C3, 2 W E5, 3 B G7, 4 W C7, 5 B G3, 6 W F4,
7 B E3, 8 W F3, 9 B F2, 10 W G4,
11 B G2, 12 W H3, 13 B E2, 14 W E4,
15 B D3, 16 W A4, 17 B B4, 18 W C6, 19 B C4, 20 W D5.

White F3 cut between E3/G3. F2 had real empty neighbors E2/F1/G2; G2 connected it to G3, E2 joined E3, and D3 joined C3. G3 had only G2/H3 after White G4, so the G2 connection mattered. C4 later joined B4 to the main lower group.

The move-10 note estimated only about 26 unsecured lower points. After move 14, the more explicit target was rows 1–2 all nine plus seven row-3 points excluding F3/H3 = 25. An upper-right F–J outline in rows 6–9 would add 16, totaling only 41. Neither group had eyes, and no secure area was claimed. This estimate correctly required more development, but depended on unprotected corner and upper boundaries.

B4/C4 contested additional lower-left space; the upper-right foothold had already been placed at move 3. This avoided relying entirely on a forty-point lower framework followed by a late unsupported invasion. The played replies do not establish that this opening is optimal.

## Upper life: preserve boundaries and connect the isolated edge stone

21 B F7, 22 W E7, 23 B G6, 24 W F8,
25 B G8, 26 W F6, 27 B G5, 28 W H4,
29 B H5, 30 W J4, 31 B J5, 32 W G9,
33 B H8, 34 W J8, 35 B H9, 36 W F9,
37 B J7, 38 W D8, 39 B H7, 40 W E9,
41 B J9 captured J8, 42 W J6, 43 B H6 captured J6.

G8 answered the F8 undercut; G5/H5/J5 secured the lower boundary before White descended farther. G9 challenged the upper boundary, but H8 then H9 prevented White's G9 and J8 stones from joining through H9. White F9 saved G9 by joining F8.

J7 put White J8 in atari at J9, but Black J7 itself was disconnected with exactly H7/J6. White D8 ignored that local fight. H7 promptly connected J7 through G7/H8; do not skip this connection when transplanting the idea.

After J9 captured J8, the two independent spaces were J8 and H6/J6. White J6 had only H6; H6 captured it and left true single-point eyes:
- J6: H6/J5/J7 boundaries.
- J8: H8/J7/J9 boundaries.
All boundaries were one connected Black group. Neither eye can be filled by White without suicide.

This supplied fifteen living area: upper rows 5–9 gave 3, 3, 4, 3, 2. The lower region still needed about thirty.

## Lower-left cleanup and life

44 W A3, 45 B B3, 46 W B1,
47 B C1, 48 W C2, 49 B D1, 50 W A5,
51 B D2, 52 W E1,
53 B B2 captured C2, 54 W A1,
55 B A2 captured A1/B1, 56 W A1,
57 B H2, 58 W C5.

White C2 put C1 in atari at D1. D1 saved it, and D2 then joined C1/D1 to the main group while putting C2 in atari at B2. White E1 ignored that atari and itself had only F1. B2 captured C2, securing true C2 with connected B2/C1/C3/D2 boundaries.

White A1 extended B1 to two stones with only A2. A2 captured both and connected directly through B2. White's repeated A1 entry had only B1. It was left enclosed while Black contested boundary points, then B1 captured it at move 85.

F1 at move 71 later captured E1 and secured true E1, bordered by D1/E2/F1. C2/E1 were already an explicit two-eye proof before final cleanup; A1 and A3/A4 provided additional eyes afterward. Lower life did not depend on a ko boundary.

## Two ignored ataris supplied the winning margin

59 B B5, 60 W B6,
61 B A6 captured A3/A4/A5, 62 W A7,
63 B A5 connected A6.

After B5, the three White left-edge stones had exactly A6. White B6 joined the central White group but ignored this atari. A6 captured three and gained A5/A7 as liberties. White A7 then left isolated Black A6 with only A5. Black A5 immediately connected it through B5; capturing alone was not enough. This preserved A3/A4 and added A5/A6 within the lower region.

64 W J2, 65 B F5, 66 W H1,
67 B E6 captured F6, 68 W D6,
69 B F6 connected E6, 70 W G1,
71 B F1 captured E1, 72 W J3.

F5 joined the living upper group and put isolated White F6 in atari at E6. White H1 ignored it. E6 captured F6, gaining D6/F6; White D6 then left isolated E6 only F6. F6 promptly joined it to F5/F7/G6. These three new area points—F5/E6/F6—expanded the upper living region from fifteen to eighteen.

White could have answered either atari rather than supplying these captures. The result validates the actual captures and connections, not an opening as forced against every reply.

## Right corner: read the recapture and then change the plan

73 B J1 captured G1/H1, 74 W H1 captured J1,
75 B D4, 76 W G1,
77 B J1 captured G1/H1, 78 W H1 captured J1,
79 B G1, 80 W B8,
81 B J1 captured H1, 82 W C9,
83 B H1 connected J1, 84 W A9,
85 B B1 captured A1, 86 W pass, 87 B pass.

The first two J1 captures each removed TWO White stones. Isolated Black J1 then had only H1. White H1 captured it and had G1/J1 as two liberties. These were legal recaptures, not ko: the preceding two White stones were not restored.

The inventory constrained the reading: do not count those captures as a secured right corner. D4 took an additional boundary point while White repeated G1. After the second exchange, G1 connected through F1/G2 and left White H1 only J1. White B8 ignored this atari.

The third J1 capture removed just ONE White stone. Here immediate White H1 would restore the preceding board, so simple ko would forbid it. This transient ko is inferred manually; the tool's returned position was after White C9 and showed ko none. No immediate recapture was attempted. H1 then connected J1 to G1/H2 and eliminated the vulnerable isolated boundary.

Before D4/G1 were resolved, the explicitly provisional outline was lower 28 + upper 18 = 46; losing both contested points would give 44, a draw. D4/G1 were secured, and the final H1/J1 gain added two, yielding 48. No arithmetic correction was needed in the final row count.

## Final life and carry forward

The final lower group had 25 stones and five territory points = 30; the upper group had 16 stones and two eyes = 18. No major Black group died. White captured only the two isolated J1 stones during the right-corner exchanges.

White's final stones were several disconnected groups, but each retained at least two separate shared eye liberties. The seven single-point White eyes had only White boundaries; an attempted Black fill captures none because every adjacent boundary group retains another liberty. Thus their disconnected appearance did not imply dead stones.

1. Retain 20k: four wins, eight losses, one draw. One win after a draw is not consistent strength.
2. Establish a second foothold while it has real room. Keep the explicit upper J6/J8 life proof and lower C2/E1 proof; do not generalize the opening as forced.
3. After every capture, inspect the new stone. A6 needed A5; E6 needed F6; J1 initially allowed a legal recapture.
4. Count contested points separately. D4/G1 mattered before passing; final 30 + 18 = 48 matched B+8.
5. Distinguish a two-stone capture from a one-stone ko. The J1/H1 exchanges changed character only after G1 became Black.
6. The three left captures and central F6 capture relied on ignored ataris. Preserve the tactical habits without claiming they will recur against stronger opponents.

All moves and variations were manual. Code only inspected current returned positions, counted groups/liberties/area, kept records and converted moves to SGF. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation was used.

# Game 11: Black vs 20k — B+2

## Opening and connections

E2 contested the lower side beneath White E3. F3 connected to G3; H3 blocked the right-side descent. Goal: improve at 9x9 Go across fresh sessions, ultimately win consistently against human-style KataGo 9d.

## Record
- Game 1: Black vs 9d, Chinese area scoring, komi 7. Lost by resignation after White move 56 (D2).
- Game 2: White vs 4k, same rules. Lost by resignation after Black move 49 (J6). No captures or numerical final score.
- Game 3: Black vs 8k, same rules. Lost by resignation after White move 64 (J5). Final captures: Black 1, White 2; no numerical final score.
- Game 4: White vs 12k, same rules. Lost by resignation after Black move 43 (F1). Final captures: Black 1, White 0; no numerical final score.
- Game 5: Black vs 20k, same rules. Lost W+12 after consecutive passes at moves 39–40. Area: Black 38, White 43 plus 7 komi. Final captures: 0 each; dead Black D8/D9/E8/E9 were removed for scoring.
- Game 6: White vs 20k, same rules. Lost B+24 after consecutive passes at moves 81–82. Area: Black 56, White 25 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 18, White 6; the nine-stone lower-left and eight-stone lower-right White groups were captured.
- Game 7: Black vs 20k, same rules. Lost W+26 after consecutive passes at moves 61–62. Area: Black 31, White 50 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 1, White 4; Black F9/G9/H9 and the invading G2 stone were captured.
- Game 8: White vs 20k, same rules. Lost B+8 after consecutive passes at moves 75–76. Area: Black 48, White 33 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 11, White 4; the eight-stone lower-left and three-stone right White groups were captured. The top group lived and repelled two invasions.
- Game 9: Black vs 20k, same rules. Lost W+42 after consecutive passes at moves 67–68. Area: Black 23, White 58 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 4, White 16; White captured fifteen left-side stones after winning the A1 ko for life. The right group lived with three independent two-point eye spaces.
- Game 10: White vs 20k, same rules. Won W+10 after consecutive passes at moves 63–64. Area: Black 39, White 42 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 0, White 4. Both White groups lived: lower 17 area with E1/D2–D3 eyes, upper 25 area with A9/C8 eyes. This is the first win in the series.
- Game 11: Black vs 20k, same rules. Won B+2 after consecutive passes at moves 58–59. Area: Black 45, White 36 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 1, White 0. Lower region scored 33 with J1/G2 eyes; upper region scored 12 with H9/J8 eyes shared by the nine-stone main group and isolated J9. No Black stone was lost. First Black win.
- Game 12: White vs 20k, same rules. Lost B+12 after consecutive passes at moves 56–57. Area: Black 50, White 31 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 9, White 0. E1/E2/E3/E4/F2/F3 were captured at move 27; H5/H6/H7 at move 49. The surviving main group had true eyes C9/D8.
- Game 13: Black vs 20k, same rules. Won B+6 after consecutive passes at moves 88–89. Area: Black 47, White 34 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 15, White 4. The unsupported H7/H8/G9/J9 invasion died; the main group lived with F3/H3 eyes. A7 captured White A5/A6/B6/B7 after B8 and White's B9 counter-atari, reopening B7 to save B8; B7 connected the new stones and the left gain supplied enough area.
- Game 14: White vs 20k, same rules. Lost B+R after Black move 61 (E9). Final captures: Black 0, White 1; no numerical final score. Eight lower-left stones were dead in the opposing-color A1/A3 shared-liberty trap; eight upper stones had only F9, and W F9, B G9 captures nine. Neither group had been physically captured at resignation. The fourteen-stone lower-right group lived with true G1/J1 eyes and secured sixteen area.
- Game 15: Black vs 20k, same rules. Lost W+8 after consecutive passes at moves 66–67. Area: Black 40, White 41 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 7, White 3. White captured E8/F7/F8; every remaining Black stone joined one living lower group with D4/J1 eyes. Black removed both lower invasions, but the lower framework itself was too small.
- Game 16: White vs 20k, same rules. Draw after consecutive passes at moves 50–51. Independent area: Black 44, White 37 plus 7 komi. Final captures: 0 each. The nineteen-stone left group lived with true C1/D2 eyes; F6/G5/G6/H4/H5 were dead but remained on the final displayed board. Manually excluding those five stones reproduced the official draw.
- Game 17: Black vs 20k, same rules. Won B+8 after consecutive passes at moves 86–87. Area: Black 48, White 33 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 16, White 2. Lower 30 lived with C2/E1 eyes and upper 18 with J6/J8 eyes. B5/A6/A5 captured three left stones and connected the capturer; F5/E6/F6 captured F6 and connected E6. Both relied on ignored ataris. The first two J1/H1 exchanges were legal recaptures after two-stone captures; after G1 became Black, the one-stone J1 capture created an inferred transient H1 ko, then H1 connected J1.
- Game 18: White vs 20k, same rules. Lost B+R after Black move 67 (J2). Final captures: Black 12, White 4; no numerical final score. Black H6 at move 57 captured eleven upper stones after White J8 filled their last outside liberty. The left sixteen stones (including isolated A1) shared true A2/B1 eyes and secured eighteen area; its lower eight were rescued by capturing A6 after an ignored atari. Five late lower-right stones remained without a second eye at resignation.
- Game 19: Black vs 20k, same rules. Lost W+10 after consecutive passes at moves 69–70. Area: Black 39, White 42 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 9, White 3. C1/D1 were captured after D2/C2; the first A1 two-stone capture allowed legal A2 recapture, the later one-stone capture made an inferred transient ko, and A2 connected A1. The thirty-one-stone main group lived with true C4/E4 eyes before capturing six left invaders, but its framework was too small.
- Game 20: White vs 20k, same rules. Lost B+16 after consecutive passes at moves 66–67. Area: Black 52, White 29 plus 7 komi. Final captures: Black 8, White 1. Black A1 captured eight lower-left stones at move 53; an A1 capture of B1/B2 would have left only one two-point eye space. The upper sixteen stones lived with J6 and J8/J9 eyes (nineteen area); the lower-right eight lived with H2/J1 (ten). Resumed after move 19; unsaved opening order is unavailable. SGF records exact setup and moves 20–67.

- Read game-013.md for its review; game-013.sgf and game-013-log.json contain all 89 moves (85 stone moves, four passes), all 45 returned positions, current-board inventories, early/late counts with a corrected arithmetic error, the one G9 ko and verified final area.
- Read game-014.md for the review; game-014.sgf and game-014-log.json contain all 61 stone moves, all 31 distinct returned positions plus resignation, current-board inventories and early counting notes. Its lower-left dead-group and upper F9/G9 proofs are manual; no final numerical score or official dead-stone adjudication occurred.
- Read game-015.md for its review; game-015.sgf and game-015-log.json contain all 67 moves (65 stone moves, two passes), all 34 play responses with current-board inventories, early counts, a corrected diagonal-liberty mistake and invalid hypothetical capture branch, and verified final area.
- Read game-016.md for its review; game-016.sgf and game-016-log.json contain all 51 moves (48 stone moves, three passes), all 26 returned positions with inventories, early counts, the corrected F1/G1 connection mistake, explicit C1/D2 life proof and independent 44–37 area count after marking the five dead right stones.
- Read game-017.md for its review; game-017.sgf and game-017-log.json contain all 87 moves (85 stone moves, two passes), all 44 returned play positions with group/liberty inventories, early/late counts, the two-stone versus one-stone J1 recapture distinction, explicit life proofs and verified 48–33 area.

- Read game-018.md for the latest review; game-018.sgf and game-018-log.json contain all 67 stone moves, all 34 returned playing positions plus resignation, current-board inventories, early counts with the F6 exclusion correction, the lower A6 rescue, exact disconnected A2/B1 shared-eye proof, the failed J8 forcing-threat correction, and manual lower-right capture proofs.

- Read game-019.md for the latest review; game-019.sgf and game-019-log.json contain all 70 moves (67 stone moves, three passes), all 35 play responses with current-board inventories, early outlines, the D1/C1 doomed-extension proof, two-stone versus one-stone A1 recapture distinction, explicit C4/E4 life proof, six-stone left capture and verified 39–42 area count.

- Read game-020.md for the latest review; game-020.sgf and game-020-log.json preserve the exact resumed position after move 19 and all 48 continuation moves (20–67), all 24 play responses, inventories, lower dead-group proof, upper J6/J8–J9 life proof, rejected F5 counter-atari, corrected G–J column-count error and verified 52–29 area. Moves 1–19 were not saved by the earlier session; no opening order is invented.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.
14. An extension must actually reach open space. In game 4, F4/F5/F6/E6 grew a connected chain without eyes. After Black E7, its remaining liberties were G1, G5, J1, J2, J3; the central escape was closed. The inventory ran every move, but did not prevent this strategic failure. Re-evaluate before the final route narrows to one point.
15. Preserving one corner boundary does not establish two eyes. Game 4's H1 prevented game 2's undercut, but Black H4 restricted the upper base. J3/J4/J5 added occupied edge stones, not eyes. At the end the thirteen-stone White group had only J1/J2: one two-point eye space. Black J2, White J1 captures one stone, Black J2 captures fourteen; this is not ko.
16. A threat may be answered by capturing its new stone. Game 4's G7 threatened Black G5/G6/H4/H5 but had only G8. Black G8 captured it and reopened G7 for three adjacent Black groups. Do not count such a threat as forcing.
17. Count playable escape points, not just raw liberties. In game 5, the top D8/D9/E8/E9 block had only D7, but Black D7 was suicide: White C7, D6 and E7 surrounded it and none would be captured. After White C8 at move 32, D9/E9 added stones without creating eyes or escape. The E8/F8/D8/C8/D9/C9/E9/F9 continuation failed.
18. A surviving framework can still be too small. Game 5's lower group scored 38 area against White's 43 plus komi. At that split, shifting six points from White to Black only draws; seven wins. Contest additional space before D6/F6 and the upper boundary close, rather than relying on a late first-line invasion.
19. Two shared liberties do not prove seki. In game 6 after move 19, White's eight-stone lower-left group and Black A2/B2 both had only A1/A3. Black A3, White A1 captured three, but Black A2 then occupied the vital point of A2/A3/B2. White A3 allows Black B2 to capture ten; White B2 allows Black A3 to capture ten. White instead played elsewhere and Black A3/B2 captured nine. The earlier claim of seki was wrong. Read beyond the first capture to the opponent's next turn.
20. A capture into a three-point eye space needs the dividing point before it supplies two eyes. In game 6, White A2 after capturing A2/A3/B2 would divide A3 and B2, but Black moved first and killed. By contrast, the upper group already had true eyes B9 (A9/B8/C9 boundaries) and E9 (D9/E8/F9 boundaries) before capturing H8/H9; all boundaries were connected White.
21. Reassess a second eye's boundary immediately after an undercut. Game 6 preserved J1 with H1/J2, but G1 required a surviving White F1 boundary. Black F2/F1/E1 connected to D1–D4, so G1 was not an eye. E4/F4/G4 led into a closed strip; Black G1/E4/F4/G4 left the eight-stone White group only J1, and Black J1 captured it. H1 alone again did not establish life.
22. Check where an atari extension ends before making the contact move. Game 6's B6 was left with only A6 by Black B7; White A6 would leave two stones with only A7, allowing Black A7 to capture both. White B8 secured the upper wall but Black A6 captured B6.
23. Repair vulnerable connections before tenuki. In game 7, F9 had only F8/G9 and was disconnected from E8. Black G2 allowed White F8/G8 to trap the top stones. F8 before tenuki is an unverified candidate connecting F9 to E8, not an established winning move.
24. A counter-atari may release the opponent when they capture first. After game 7's Black F7 at move 47, White F8/G8 had only H8, but Black F9/G9 had only H9. White H9 could capture two and open F9/G9 for the invaders. Actual White J9 at move 52 captured F9/G9/H9 and reopened F9/G9/H9. Black's attempted chase did not force a capture.
25. A diagonal framework also needs a concrete area count. Game 7's vague estimate of about 45 was unsupported; the later row count gave only 38 potential points even with the top intact. Losing seven top points left 31. The main group did live: G6 (F6/G5/G7/H6 boundaries) and J6 (H6/J5/J7 boundaries) were independent true eyes after H7 connected all boundaries.
26. Empty prospective eye points need secured boundaries and enough turns. Game 7's G2 invasion lost its right route to White H2 and its left route to White F2. Then Black G1, White F1, Black H1, White J1 would capture three. Black abandoned G2 instead; White G1 captured it. Do not treat the G2 entry as a proven living pattern.
27. Three corner approaches are not three living bases. In game 8, White C7/C3/G7/E7 built a surviving top wall, but C3 was left alone until move 22. After Black A3, the lower-left had only E4/D3/B2/B1. C1 protected the right first-line boundary but did not preserve the left boundary. Black E2 connected E3 to D2/D1; White E4, Black F4 closed the last central route, leaving only B2/B1. Black A2/B1/B2 captured eight. Develop a second base before the wall and undercuts close it; no saving replacement is verified.
28. An extension into one temporary liberty is not an escape. In game 8, White E4 added F4, which Black immediately occupied. The corner could not save the group: after move 35, W B2, B A2, W B1, B A1 captures ten. Alternatively W B1, B B2 leaves only A1; W A1 is legal but leaves only A2, where Black connects B2 to A3 and captures ten. Do not confuse this legal one-liberty extension with suicide.
29. An edge strip also needs an outside boundary. Game 8's H3/H2/H1 had only J3/J2/J1 after Black H4/G2/G1. J4 was unsecured, so these were not two eyes. Black J3/J2/J1 captured all three; White J1 was suicide because Black J2/J3 retained J4. Do not reuse this late entry as a living pattern.
30. Game 8's top main group had true eyes D7 (C7/D6/E7/D8) and E9 (D9/E8/F9), all boundaries connected White. B7/C8/C9 then contained A7/B8; A8 and B9 captured them. H8/G9/J9 captured H9. Rebuilding liberties after captures preserved the top, but its 33 area still lost to 48 plus the komi adjustment. Life and sufficient area remain separate tests.

31. Game 9's capture of White A4/A5 at move 45 left Black only A4/A5: one two-point eye. Black A1 later captured A2, but A1 itself had only A2. After B A5 captured the invading A4 stone, W A2 captured A1 and created a ko at A1; the fifteen-stone main group had only A4. No adequate forcing ko threat was established. B H5 connected the right side, but W A4 ignored it and captured fifteen. Captures and connected stones did not establish a second unconditional eye.
32. In game 9, White B1 undermined the left first-line eye boundary before the A4 invasion. B2/B3 and later B4/B5 did not fix it. Reconsider development before those undercuts and the vital eye-space invasion; no saving replacement is verified. The eleven-stone left group after move 35 had only an eighteen-point geometric outline, including unsecured A1/A2/A3/A4/A5/B4/B5, so saving that outline alone would not establish a winning total.
33. Game 9's right group lived after H5 connected its parts and H1/J3/J5 secured independent two-point eye spaces J1/J2 (H1/H2/J3 boundaries) and H4/J4 (G4/H3/H5/J3/J5 boundaries). J8 later secured a third space J6/J7 (H6/H7/J5/J8 boundaries). All boundaries were connected Black. Its 23 area still lost badly; H1 alone was not the life proof.

34. Game 10 won as White with two living groups: lower 17 area plus upper 25 = 42, against Black 39 plus White's 7 komi. A small living base can anchor a sufficient total if a second base develops before the board closes. C7 at move 14 supplied an upper foothold; after lower life at move 30, E7/G7/C6/D6 expanded the top. This is one successful continuation, not a proven optimal opening.
35. In game 10 after Black E1 at move 21, immediate White D1 would have only C1, and Black C1 could capture it and reopen D1. White F1 first put E1 in atari; Black ignored it. White D1 then captured E1 and gained E1 as a liberty, and C1 captured C2/D2/D3 after another ignored atari. The opened liberty changed the tactic. Black's mistakes do not establish a forced opening win.
36. Game 10's captures did not alone prove life. F2 connected isolated F1, then C2 joined C1/D1 to the main group. E1 (D1/E2/F1 boundaries) and D2/D3 (D1/C2/E2/C3/E3/D4 boundaries) were then independent true eye spaces, with every boundary connected White. Capturing B1 by A1 after move 27 would instead have introduced a ko through isolated A1; unconditional life was secured elsewhere.
37. Game 10 repaired short-liberty stones promptly: A8–B8, F8–E8, G7–G8. After Black F7 at move 47, White F6 would have had only G6; Black G6 could capture it and reopen F6. Actual White F8 had E8/G8/F9, put F7 in atari, and connected through E8 after Black F6. Check the new atari stone's own liberties.
38. Game 10's upper eyes were A9 (A8/B9 boundaries) and C8 (B8/C7/D8/C9 boundaries). B9 connected to B8 before C9 joined through B9; C9 is only diagonal to B8/D8. Do not mistake a diagonal boundary arrangement for a connected life proof. The final count was verified, but the detailed row count came late; count earlier around moves 10–16 next game.

39. Game 11 counted an unsecured 48-point outline after move 10, then revised it as White reduced the right side. After move 48, upper 12 plus lower 32 was only 44, insufficient for Black to win. Actual B6/B5/A5 added and preserved B6, giving lower 33 and total 45. The count changed the plan before passing. This gain is verified for the played replies, not forced against every reply.
40. Game 11's B J9 at move 45 had only H9 and put White J8 in atari at H8. White E6 ignored both ataris. B H8 captured J8 and opened J8 as a SECOND liberty for isolated J9. After W J6, the nine-stone main upper group and J9 each had exactly H9/J8. H9 boundaries G9/H8/J9 and J8 boundaries H8/J7/J9 are all Black. W at either eye captures neither boundary group, because both retain the other eye, and is suicide. These two same-color groups live unconditionally despite being disconnected. This is not game 6's opposing-color shared liberties or game 9's one-liberty ko boundary. NEVER fill H9 or J8 to connect J9: the joined group then has only one eye.
41. Game 11's upper rescue depended on W E6 ignoring the atari, not a forced winning sequence. W H9 could capture J9 immediately at move 46; B H8 then captures three into bent-three H9/J9/J8, but White moves first and can occupy dividing J9. Do not count that alternative alive. Preserve upper eye space earlier; no single replacement is verified.
42. Game 11's lower group secured true eyes J1 (H1/J2 boundaries) and G2 (F2/G3/H2/G1 boundaries) after H1 then G1 connected all boundaries. The final 19 stones plus 14 territory gave 33 area. Black completed this proof after White's first pass before accepting B+2. Prompt connections J2–H2, E2–F2, G9–G8, H6–H7 and B6–B5 preserved every Black stone.

43. Game 12 inspected liberties every contact move but still extended into a closed strip. After B F4 at move 21, White E3/E4/F3 had only E2/F2. W F2, B G2 left E2/F1; W E2, B F1 left only E1. W E1 was legal but left six stones only D1; B D1 connected to D2 and captured six. No eyes or escape were created. Reconsider before E4/F3 and the enclosing F4/G2/F1 replies; merely swapping E2 for F2 is not a verified rescue.
44. Game 12's H5/H6/H7 invasion had no demonstrated life plan. Black H4/H8 owned both outside edge boundaries; G5 connected the center and top Black chains and left White only J5/J6/J7. B J7/J6/J5 captured three. After B J6, W J5 would have only J4; B J4 joins H4 and captures four, without ko. Three connected edge liberties do not supply two eyes, and needing more area does not justify counting an unsupported invasion as a base.
45. Game 12's early unsecured outline was 42 (A–D columns plus E1/E2/E3/E7/E8/E9), but Black's D-line separated the lower E-stones and occupied that outline. After the lower capture and top reductions, the left outline was about 33; final lower-boundary settlement left 31. The main group lived with C9 (B9/C8/D9 boundaries) and D8 (C8/D7/E8/D9 boundaries), all connected White after C8/D9/B8/B9. D9 connected through E9, not diagonal C8/D7. Life and enough area remain separate requirements.

46. Game 13's H7/H8/G9/J9 entry had no demonstrated two-eye or connection plan. After J9 captured White H9, White F9 left isolated G9 only H9. Connecting by H9 would leave only J7/J8, one two-point eye space. White H9 captured G9 into ko, J8 captured J9, and J7 captured H7/H8. Black abandoned four stones instead of adding a doomed strip. Do not reuse this as a living pattern or let the overall win validate it.
47. Game 13 correctly read a counter-atari through the capture. After White A5/A6, White A5/A6/B6/B7 had exactly A7/B8. Black B8 put it in atari, White B9 left Black B8 only A8, but Black A7 captured four and reopened B7 as B8's SECOND liberty. Black B7 then joined A7 and B8 directly to C7 and the living main group. The capture changed the inventory; no ko was involved. Earlier White play created this opportunity, so it is not a forced opening win.
48. Game 13's main group had independent true eyes F3 (E3/F2/F4/G3 boundaries) and H3 (G3/H2/H4/J3 boundaries) after F2 and later J4/J2 joined all boundaries. The late left capture expanded an already living group. Final captures also supplied A6, D2, H1 and A2/B2 eyes. Black finished capturing dead A6/H1 before passing; final 40 stones plus seven territory = 47.
49. Game 13 counted a 45-point unsecured outline after move 10, but White D8/C8/B7/B6 reduced the main outline to about 37. After the right recovery, the note claiming 42 was an arithmetic error: rows 1–3 gave 27, row 4 six, row 5 FOUR, rows 6/7 two each, total41. White A5 reduced that outline to40; capturing four and adding A7/B8 gave46, A8 gave47. Correct row counts explicitly; final B+6 matched the independent count. Earlier top-left development remains hypothetical, with no verified single replacement.

50. Game 14's B4 repair at move 16 allowed Black C5 to join B5/C6 and close the lower group's central route. B2/A4/B1/A5 made connections but no eyes; Black A6 left eight White stones and Black A2 sharing only A1/A3. ## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.
14. An extension must actually reach open space. In game 4, F4/F5/F6/E6 grew a connected chain without eyes. After Black E7, its remaining liberties were G1, G5, J1, J2, J3; the central escape was closed. The inventory ran every move, but did not prevent this strategic failure. Re-evaluate before the final route narrows to one point.
15. Preserving one corner boundary does not establish two eyes. Game 4's H1 prevented game 2's undercut, but Black H4 restricted the upper base. J3/J4/J5 added occupied edge stones, not eyes. At the end the thirteen-stone White group had only J1/J2: one two-point eye space. Black J2, White J1 captures one stone, Black J2 captures fourteen; this is not ko.
16. A threat may be answered by capturing its new stone. Game 4's G7 threatened Black G5/G6/H4/H5 but had only G8. Black G8 captured it and reopened G7 for three adjacent Black groups. Do not count such a threat as forcing.
17. Count playable escape points, not just raw liberties. In game 5, the top D8/D9/E8/E9 block had only D7, but Black D7 was suicide: White C7, D6 and E7 surrounded it and none would be captured. After White C8 at move 32, D9/E9 added stones without creating eyes or escape. The E8/F8/D8/C8/D9/C9/E9/F9 continuation failed.
18. A surviving framework can still be too small. Game 5's lower group scored 38 area against White's 43 plus komi. At that split, shifting six points from White to Black only draws; seven wins. Contest additional space before D6/F6 and the upper boundary close, rather than relying on a late first-line invasion.
19. Two shared liberties do not prove seki. In game 6 after move 19, White's eight-stone lower-left group and Black A2/B2 both had only A1/A3. Black A3, White A1 captured three, but Black A2 then occupied the vital point of A2/A3/B2. White A3 allows Black B2 to capture ten; White B2 allows Black A3 to capture ten. White instead played elsewhere and Black A3/B2 captured nine. The earlier claim of seki was wrong. Read beyond the first capture to the opponent's next turn.
20. A capture into a three-point eye space needs the dividing point before it supplies two eyes. In game 6, White A2 after capturing A2/A3/B2 would divide A3 and B2, but Black moved first and killed. By contrast, the upper group already had true eyes B9 (A9/B8/C9 boundaries) and E9 (D9/E8/F9 boundaries) before capturing H8/H9; all boundaries were connected White.
21. Reassess a second eye's boundary immediately after an undercut. Game 6 preserved J1 with H1/J2, but G1 required a surviving White F1 boundary. Black F2/F1/E1 connected to D1–D4, so G1 was not an eye. E4/F4/G4 led into a closed strip; Black G1/E4/F4/G4 left the eight-stone White group only J1, and Black J1 captured it. H1 alone again did not establish life.
22. Check where an atari extension ends before making the contact move. Game 6's B6 was left with only A6 by Black B7; White A6 would leave two stones with only A7, allowing Black A7 to capture both. White B8 secured the upper wall but Black A6 captured B6.
23. Repair vulnerable connections before tenuki. In game 7, F9 had only F8/G9 and was disconnected from E8. Black G2 allowed White F8/G8 to trap the top stones. F8 before tenuki is an unverified candidate connecting F9 to E8, not an established winning move.

White H9 could capture two and open F9/G9 for the invaders. Actual White J9 at move 52 captured F9/G9/H9 and reopened F9/G9/H9. Black's attempted chase did not force a capture.

Losing seven top points left 31. The main group did live: G6 (F6/G5/G7/H6 boundaries) and J6 (H6/J5/J7 boundaries) were independent true eyes after H7 connected all boundaries.

Then Black G1, White F1, Black H1, White J1 would capture three. Black abandoned G2 instead; White G1 captured it. Do not treat the G2 entry as a proven living pattern.

Black E2 connected E3 to D2/D1; White E4, Black F4 closed the last central route, leaving only B2/B1. Black A2/B1/B2 captured eight. Develop a second base before the wall and undercuts close it; no saving replacement is verified.

The corner could not save the group: after move 35, W B2, B A2, W B1, B A1 captures ten. Alternatively W B1, B B2 leaves only A1; W A1 is legal but leaves only A2, where Black connects B2 to A3 and captures ten. Do not confuse this legal one-liberty extension with suicide.

Black J3/J2/J1 captured all three; White J1 was suicide bec…3280 tokens truncated…F5/G4; W at either point adds no liberty, and Black at the other captures six. ## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.
14. An extension must actually reach open space. In game 4, F4/F5/F6/E6 grew a connected chain without eyes. After Black E7, its remaining liberties were G1, G5, J1, J2, J3; the central escape was closed. The inventory ran every move, but did not prevent this strategic failure. Re-evaluate before the final route narrows to one point.
15. Preserving one corner boundary does not establish two eyes. Game 4's H1 prevented game 2's undercut, but Black H4 restricted the upper base. J3/J4/J5 added occupied edge stones, not eyes. At the end the thirteen-stone White group had only J1/J2: one two-point eye space. Black J2, White J1 captures one stone, Black J2 captures fourteen; this is not ko.
16. A threat may be answered by capturing its new stone. Game 4's G7 threatened Black G5/G6/H4/H5 but had only G8. Black G8 captured it and reopened G7 for three adjacent Black groups. Do not count such a threat as forcing.
17. Count playable escape points, not just raw liberties. In game 5, the top D8/D9/E8/E9 block had only D7, but Black D7 was suicide: White C7, D6 and E7 surrounded it and none would be captured. After White C8 at move 32, D9/E9 added stones without creating eyes or escape. The E8/F8/D8/C8/D9/C9/E9/F9 continuation failed.
18. A surviving framework can still be too small. Game 5's lower group scored 38 area against White's 43 plus komi. At that split, shifting six points from White to Black only draws; seven wins. Contest additional space before D6/F6 and the upper boundary close, rather than relying on a late first-line invasion.
19. Two shared liberties do not prove seki. In game 6 after move 19, White's eight-stone lower-left group and Black A2/B2 both had only A1/A3. Black A3, White A1 captured three, but Black A2 then occupied the vital point of A2/A3/B2. White A3 allows Black B2 to capture ten; White B2 allows Black A3 to capture ten. White instead played elsewhere and Black A3/B2 captured nine. The earlier claim of seki was wrong. Read beyond the first capture to the opponent's next turn.
20. A capture into a three-point eye space needs the dividing point before it supplies two eyes. In game 6, White A2 after capturing A2/A3/B2 would divide A3 and B2, but Black moved first and killed. By contrast, the upper group already had true eyes B9 (A9/B8/C9 boundaries) and E9 (D9/E8/F9 boundaries) before capturing H8/H9; all boundaries were connected White.
21. Reassess a second eye's boundary immediately after an undercut. Game 6 preserved J1 with H1/J2, but G1 required a surviving White F1 boundary. Black F2/F1/E1 connected to D1–D4, so G1 was not an eye. E4/F4/G4 led into a closed strip; Black G1/E4/F4/G4 left the eight-stone White group only J1, and Black J1 captured it. H1 alone again did not establish life.
22. Check where an atari extension ends before making the contact move. Game 6's B6 was left with only A6 by Black B7; White A6 would leave two stones with only A7, allowing Black A7 to capture both. White B8 secured the upper wall but Black A6 captured B6.
23. Repair vulnerable connections before tenuki. In game 7, F9 had only F8/G9 and was disconnected from E8. Black G2 allowed White F8/G8 to trap the top stones. F8 before tenuki is an unverified candidate connecting F9 to E8, not an established winning move.
24. A counter-atari may release the opponent when they capture first. After game 7's Black F7 at move 47, White F8/G8 had only H8, but Black F9/G9 had only H9. White H9 could capture two and open F9/G9 for the invaders. Actual White J9 at move 52 captured F9/G9/H9 and reopened F9/G9/H9. Black's attempted chase did not force a capture.
25. A diagonal framework also needs a concrete area count. Game 7's vague estimate of about 45 was unsupported; the later row count gave only 38 potential points even with the top intact. Losing seven top points left 31. The main group did live: G6 (F6/G5/G7/H6 boundaries) and J6 (H6/J5/J7 boundaries) were independent true eyes after H7 connected all boundaries.
26. Empty prospective eye points need secured boundaries and enough turns. Game 7's G2 invasion lost its right route to White H2 and its left route to White F2. Then Black G1, White F1, Black H1, White J1 would capture three. Black abandoned G2 instead; White G1 captured it. Do not treat the G2 entry as a proven living pattern.

Black E2 connected E3 to D2/D1; White E4, Black F4 closed the last central route, leaving only B2/B1. Black A2/B1/B2 captured eight. Develop a second base before the wall and undercuts close it; no saving replacement is verified.

The corner could not save the group: after move 35, W B2, B A2, W B1, B A1 captures ten. Alternatively W B1, B B2 leaves only A1; W A1 is legal but leaves only A2, where Black connects B2 to A3 and captures ten. Do not confuse this legal one-liberty extension with suicide.
